introduction-the-language-of-performance.core: Big O describes how an algorithm's time or memory grows as input size n grows, ignoring hardware and constants. It lets engineers compare approaches before writing code and predict whether a solution survives 10× or 1,000× more data.

first_principles.problem: Two solutions both finish instantly on 100 items, but one takes hours on 10 million.
truths: Hardware speed varies; growth rate doesn't.
derivation: Count **operations as a function of n**.

analogy.title: Comparing travel by how time scales with distance
analogy.story: Walking, driving and flying all handle 1 km fine; at 1,000 km the difference is everything.
analogy.breaks: Travel has fixed setup costs like airport security; Big O hides constants that matter for small n.

example.title: Duplicate check
example.outcome: the scalable approach chosen up front.

check.q: Why ignore constants in Big O?
check.a: For large n the growth rate dominates, and constants depend on hardware and implementation details.

the-rules-of-simplification.core: Simplify Big O by dropping constants (O(2n) → O(n)), dropping lower-order terms (O(n² + n) → O(n²)), adding sequential steps (O(a + b)), multiplying nested ones (O(a·b)), and keeping different inputs as different variables.

first_principles.problem: Candidates write O(3n² + 5n + 2) or wrongly merge two arrays' sizes into one n.
derivation: **Separate variables** for separate inputs (O(a·b), not O(n²)).

analogy.title: Estimating a road trip by the longest leg
analogy.story: For a cross-country drive, the 5-minute drive to the motorway barely matters.
analogy.breaks: On a short trip the 'small' legs dominate, just as constants matter for small n.

check.q: What's the complexity of iterating array A then nested over A and B?
check.a: O(a + a·b), which simplifies to O(a·b).

the-big-o-zoo-common-complexities.core: Common classes from fastest to slowest: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear scan, O(n log n) efficient sort, O(n²) nested pairs, O(2ⁿ) subsets, O(n!) permutations. Recognising which class a pattern belongs to tells you if it's feasible for the given constraints.

first_principles.problem: With n = 10⁵, a candidate proposes an O(n²) solution that needs 10¹⁰ operations.
truths: ~10⁸ simple operations per second is a rough budget.
Each pattern has a typical class.
Constraints hint at the expected complexity.

analogy.title: A zoo from snails to cheetahs
analogy.story: Each animal has a characteristic speed; know which one you're riding before the race.
analogy.breaks: Animals have fixed speeds; algorithm time also depends on n.

example.title: Reading constraints
flow: So target sorting, heaps or binary search

check.q: Which class does generating all subsets belong to?
check.a: O(2ⁿ), since each element is in or out.

deep-dive-understanding-logarithmic-time.core: O(log n) arises when each step cuts the remaining problem by a constant fraction, usually half. log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30, so halving search finds an item among a billion in about 30 steps. It appears in binary search, balanced trees, heaps and repeated doubling.

first_principles.problem: Searching a sorted list of a billion IDs one by one takes a billion comparisons.
truths: Halving repeatedly reaches 1 in log₂ n steps.
Tree height in balanced trees is log n.
derivation: Ask: **does each step shrink the problem by a factor?**

analogy.title: Guessing a number with higher/lower hints
analogy.story: Always guess the middle, and you'll find any number from 1 to a million in 20 guesses.
analogy.breaks: The game needs honest hints; binary search needs sorted (monotonic) data.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: 1,000× more data costs only 10 more steps.

check.q: Roughly how many steps does binary search take on 1 million items?

best-average-and-worst-case.core: An algorithm's running time can depend on the input arrangement. Best case is the luckiest input, average case is the expected value over typical inputs, and worst case is the guarantee. Interviews and SLAs usually care about worst case, but average case explains why Quicksort and hash maps are fast in practice.

first_principles.problem: Quicksort is called O(n log n), yet it degrades to O(n²) on already-sorted input with a naive pivot.
truths: Randomisation can make worst cases unlikely.

analogy.title: Commute time
analogy.story: Best: all green lights. Average: typical traffic. Worst: an accident on the motorway.
analogy.breaks: Traffic isn't adversarial; attackers can deliberately craft worst-case inputs (hash flooding).

check.a: When pivots repeatedly split badly, e.g. a first-element pivot on already sorted input.

space-complexity-ram-matters-too.core: Space complexity counts extra memory an algorithm needs as n grows: auxiliary data structures and the recursion call stack (input usually excluded). Trading space for time (memoisation, hash maps) is common, but memory limits and cache effects make space a real constraint.

first_principles.problem: A solution is O(n) time but allocates an n×n matrix and runs out of memory at n = 10⁵.
truths: Space and time often trade off.

analogy.title: Desk space while working
analogy.story: Spreading papers out speeds work but needs a bigger desk.
analogy.breaks: Desks don't overflow and crash; a deep recursion overflows the stack.

example.title: Reverse an array
flow: Swap ends in place → O(1) space

steps.label: Choice
steps.detail: In place when memory is tight.

check.q: What's the space complexity of recursive DFS on a path-shaped tree of n nodes?
check.a: O(n), because the call stack reaches depth n.

recursive-complexity.core: Analyse recursion by drawing the recursion tree: total work = (number of calls) × (work per call), or the sum per level. Branching factor b and depth d give roughly O(bᵈ) calls; the Master Theorem solves divide-and-conquer recurrences like T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).

first_principles.problem: Naive recursive Fibonacci looks simple but takes seconds for n = 40.
truths: Each call may spawn several more.
Depth is how many times the input shrinks.
derivation: Apply the **Master Theorem** for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).

analogy.title: A phone tree
analogy.story: Each person calls two others, so the number of calls doubles at every level.
analogy.breaks: In a phone tree people aren't called twice; in naive recursion the same subproblem repeats.

points: Master Theorem for divide and conquer.

check.q: What's the complexity of merge sort by the Master Theorem?
check.a: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n log n).

amortized-analysis-the-rent-concept.core: Amortised analysis averages cost over a sequence of operations. A dynamic array's append is usually O(1) but occasionally O(n) when it doubles and copies. Because doubling makes those copies geometrically rare, n appends cost O(n) total, so O(1) amortised each.

first_principles.problem: Candidates claim list.append is O(n) because resizing copies everything.
truths: Average over a sequence differs from average over inputs.

analogy.title: Rent versus buying furniture
analogy.story: You pay a big sum occasionally for furniture, but spread over months it's a small monthly cost.
analogy.breaks: Real-time systems care about the single big payment, i.e. the worst-case latency spike.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Geometric growth makes rare expensive work cheap on average.

check.q: Why must dynamic arrays grow geometrically for O(1) amortised append?
check.a: Fixed increments cause a copy every k appends, giving O(n²) total; doubling keeps total copies under 2n.
